consonants.note: voiceless bilabial stop; aspirated word-initially
voiced bilabial stop
voiceless dental/alveolar stop; aspirated word-initially
voiced alveolar stop; often weakened intervocalically in casual speech
voiceless velar stop; aspirated word-initially; before front vowels e,i,y,ä,ö → /ɕ/
voiced velar stop; before front vowels e,i,y,ä,ö → /j/ (see /j/ row); word-finally devoices to /k/ in many words (dag → /dɑːk/)
voiceless labiodental fricative
voiced labiodental fricative
voiceless alveolar sibilant
the sj-sound — a simultaneous velar+labial fricative; highly variable by dialect (may sound like /ʃ/ or /x/); the headline messy case in Swedish spelling
the tj-sound; voiceless alveolo-palatal fricative; further forward than English 'sh'
glottal fricative; h is silent in hj- clusters (hjälpa → /jɛlpa/)
palatal approximant; in dj/gj/hj/lj clusters only the /j/ is pronounced — the first letter is silent
bilabial nasal
alveolar nasal; assimilates to /ŋ/ before /k/ and /g/
velar nasal; the g in ng is silent (unlike English 'finger'); nk → /ŋk/
alveolar lateral approximant; merges with preceding r to form retroflex /ɭ/ in rl clusters
alveolar trill or tap in central/northern Sweden; uvular /ʀ/ in southern Sweden. Triggers retroflexion of following t/d/n/l/s
retroflex stop from r+t assimilation; only in r-dialects (not southern/Scanian Swedish)
retroflex stop from r+d assimilation; only in r-dialects
retroflex nasal from r+n assimilation; only in r-dialects
retroflex lateral from r+l assimilation; only in r-dialects
retroflex fricative from r+s assimilation; sounds like English 'sh' but retroflex; only in r-dialects

vowels.note: close front unrounded, long; long syllable = single consonant follows (bil vs bill)

spellings: i (closed syllable, before double consonant or cluster)
vowels.note: near-close front unrounded, short; vit /viːt/ (long i) vs vitt /vɪtː/ (short i)
close-mid front unrounded, long; de (they) is spelled with e but pronounced /dɔm/ in normal speech — the spelling is historical
open-mid front unrounded, short; e and ä both yield /ɛ/ in closed syllables in many dialects
open-mid front unrounded, long; some educated Stockholm speakers merge this with /eː/
open front (or central) unrounded, long; one of the most frequent vowels in Swedish
open front unrounded, short; dag /daːɡ/ vs dagg (dew) /daɡː/
close back rounded, long; highly protruded lips — unlike English /uː/. Letter o = /uː/ in many common words (bort, stor, blomma); bok is sometimes cited but has variable realization across dialects
near-close back rounded, short; och is commonly /ɔk/ or /ʊk/ depending on speaker

spellings: o (words with historical short ŏ, varies by word)
vowels.note: close-mid back rounded, long; the letter å always represents this vowel (long) or its short counterpart
open-mid back rounded, short; short counterpart to /oː/
close front rounded, long; like French 'u' or German 'ü'; one of Swedish's distinctive vowels; round lips as for /uː/ but tongue forward as for /iː/
near-close front rounded, short; ny /yː/ vs nytt /ʏtː/
close-mid front rounded, long; like German 'ö' or French 'eu'; round lips as for /oː/ but tongue forward; one of Swedish's three extra letters
open-mid front rounded, short; söt /søːt/ (long) vs möss /mœsː/ (short)

schwa — a reduced, central vowel in unstressed syllables; the -e in pojke and the vowel in -en/-er/-et endings are all reduced toward /ə/ in natural speech. Not a phonemic contrast in Swedish but important for natural-sounding output.

pitch_accent.description: Swedish has two lexical tones called accent 1 (acute) and accent 2 (grave). Most polysyllabic words have accent 2; monosyllables and words derived from monosyllabic stems have accent 1. Confusing them rarely causes misunderstanding but is immediately noticeable.

accent1.name: Accent 1 (acute / single tone)
accent1.description: A single falling tone on the stressed syllable. Common in monosyllables and words derived from monosyllables by adding -en/-et.

accent2.name: Accent 2 (grave / double tone)
accent2.description: A rise-fall melody spread over the stressed syllable and the next; sounds like a 'singing' quality. Default for most native polysyllabic words.

examples.note: same spelling as 'the duck' but different tone

pitch_accent.note: Accent realization varies greatly by dialect — Stockholm has falling+rising; Gothenburg has a distinctive lilt; southern Sweden (Scania) lacks the distinction entirely. Focus on recognizing that it exists; perfect the melody with a tutor.

prosody_rules.description: In a stressed syllable, vowel length and the following consonant length are always complementary: long vowel + short consonant, OR short vowel + long consonant. A stressed syllable is never short vowel + short consonant.

examples.note: short /ɪ/ + long /lː/ — though this spelling is rare, the pattern applies to all stressed syllables

prosody_rules.rule: Double consonant = preceding vowel is short
prosody_rules.description: A doubled consonant letter (tt, ll, nn, ss, etc.) signals that the preceding stressed vowel is short, and the consonant itself is held longer. This applies across the board — it is the general spelling rule, not word-specific.

The letters k, g, and sk change pronunciation before front vowels (e, i, y, ä, ö). This is a positional rule, not a separate letter: k → /ɕ/, g → /j/, sk → /ɧ/. See the /ɕ/, /j/, and /ɧ/ rows for spelling details.
